findings.title: Item resume never holds the project run lock while the body runs
findings.description: `resume_item` takes `project_run_lock(cwd)` inside an `ExitStack` and then calls `await _resume_locked(...)` — which awaits `run_body(...)` — *inside* the `with ExitStack() as stack:` block, so the lock is held for the whole body run. That part is correct. The defect is on the CLI side: `handle_item_resume` (src/squadron/cli/commands/run_item.py:82-104) calls `asyncio.run(resume_item(...))` and the inner `run_body` calls `_run_pipeline_sdk(...)` — but `_run_pipeline_sdk` is **not** wrapped in `_locked`. So the item body itself is fine (lock held by `resume_item`), yet the *same* `resume_item` path can also be entered through `run.py` where `_locked` is used for normal runs. The two entry points therefore use different locking strategies for the same mutation, and the CLI's `run_item` path never goes through `_take_run_lock`/`pipeline_mutates` — a non-mutating pipeline resumed via `--item` still takes the lock, while the mutating one takes it too, but through two different code paths with different exit codes (`ResumeExit.REJECTED` = 2 vs. `typer.Exit(2)`), duplicating the lock logic in `run.py:_take_run_lock` and `item_resume.resume_item`. Consider extracting a single lock-acquisition helper used by both.

findings.title: `resume_item` catches `OSError` and reports it as a report-write failure regardless of cause
`_finish_each_report` on a halt appends duplicate records for an item resume
findings.description: On the item-resume path, `_execute_each_step` runs with `items = [item_rerun.item]`, so `in_flight` is `(0, item)`. If the body raises `GitEnvironmentError`, `_finish_each_report` calls `_add_record(report, BatchItemRecord.from_item(...), item_rerun)`, which calls `item_rerun.replace(record)` — replacing the item's record in place (correct). But when `halt is not None`, it then does `report.records.extend(BatchItemRecord.not_run(i, pos, reason) for pos, i in unreached)` — with `items[position+1:]` empty for a resume, so no harm there. The real problem is the non-resume path: `BatchItemRecord.from_item(item, position, [], reason, flag_kind=FlagKind.STEP_FAILED)` hard-codes `STEP_FAILED` for the halted item, discarding the real cause. The diff's own test expects `- 106 Other Thing — step_failed; working tree not clean: unrelated.txt`, i.e. the git fault is now recorded as a generic step failure rather than a distinct kind, and `FlagKind` has no member for "run halted" — a consumer routing on `flagKind` cannot distinguish an environment halt from an ordinary step failure.

findings.title: `order_by_dependencies` is O(n²) and recomputes dependents on every pop
findings.description: For every popped item the function scans the full `indices` list to find dependents (`for index in indices: if index not in placed and indices[pos] in needs[index]`). With a large plan (hundreds of slices) this is quadratic in the number of items. A reverse-adjacency map (`dependents[index] -> set`) would make it linear. This runs on the hot path of every `implement-plan` batch (source evaluation) and again on every item resume.

findings.title: `order_by_dependencies` raises `ValueError` on a dependency cycle instead of failing at the source boundary with a clear error
findings.description: The `try/except ValueError` around `order_by_dependencies` logs and re-raises the raw `ValueError`. `evaluate_each_source` is called from `_execute_each_step` and from `_select_item` in `item_resume.py:280`; neither converts it into a typed, user-facing failure, so a cyclic plan produces an unhandled traceback rather than a clean pipeline-level error naming the plan. The executor's `_execute_step` has no handling for `ValueError` from source evaluation.

findings.title: `_find_cycle` can loop forever if `needs` contains a self-dependency
findings.description:
```python
following = min(needs[path[-1]])
if following in path:
    return [*path[path.index(following):], following]
path.append(following)
```
For a self-dependency (`item 5` depends on `5`), `needs[5] = {5}`; `following = 5`, `5 in path` is True immediately, so it returns `[5, 5]`. That case is fine. However, if `needs[path[-1]]` is empty for an unplaced node (which cannot normally happen, since a node with no needs is placed), `min()` raises `ValueError: min() arg is an empty sequence` — an unrelated, uninformative error replacing the intended "dependency cycle" message. The invariant is not asserted anywhere.

findings.title: `BatchReport.load` silently accepts a report whose `items` entries are not dicts
findings.description: `items = cast(list[dict[str, object]], report["items"])` is a bare `cast` — a no-op at runtime. If `items` is not a list (e.g. a dict or a string), the comprehension `BatchItemRecord.from_json(item)` will raise `TypeError` (caught → `BatchReportLoadError`, acceptable). But if an item is a *string*, `from_json` calls `data.get(key)` → `AttributeError`, which is **not** in the caught tuple `(KeyError, TypeError, ValueError)` and therefore escapes as an unhandled `AttributeError` instead of `BatchReportLoadError`. The same applies to `from_json` receiving a non-dict. This is the trust boundary for a file that is read back from disk, and the project's Python rules require Pydantic or equivalent validation at external boundaries.

findings.title: `BatchItemRecord.from_json` coerces missing required fields into misleading values
findings.description: `values = {attr: data.get(key) for attr, key in _JSON_KEYS.items()}` — for a record missing `"index"`, `str(values["index"])` yields the literal string `"None"` rather than failing. A malformed report therefore loads as a record with index `"None"`, name `"None"`, outcome `"None"` → `ItemOutcome("None")` raises `ValueError` (caught), so `outcome` is the one field that fails loudly. But `index`/`name` do not, and a record with a valid `outcome` but missing `index` would be silently stored as index `"None"`, which then never matches any requested item index and silently breaks item resume selection. The trust boundary should validate required fields explicitly.

findings.title: `TaskEntry` parsing now requires `completed`/`total` keys, breaking older cf output
findings.description: `list_tasks` now does `completed=int(e["completed"])` and `total=int(e["total"])` — direct subscript, unlike every other field in the same comprehension which uses `.get(...)` with a default. If `cf list tasks --json` does not emit these keys (an older cf, or a plan without task items), this raises `KeyError` out of `list_tasks`, which is not a `ContextForgeError` and therefore escapes the client's error contract — callers that catch `ContextForgeError` will not handle it, and the batch source `_cf_slices_ready_to_implement` will crash instead of skipping the slice. The rest of the class consistently degrades with defaults; this should be `int(e.get("completed", 0))`.

findings.title: `cf.slices_ready_to_implement` flags a slice as `not_ready` when all its tasks are checked, but the reason is misleading
findings.description: The reason string is `"all tasks checked but slice not marked complete"`, but the flag kind is `FlagKind.NOT_READY`. `_not_ready_reason` documents this as "Implemented and merged but not closed out; rerunning would reimplement it." A `not_ready` kind plus this reason will route the item to a "not ready" bucket in a consumer, when the actual state is "already implemented, awaiting close-out". This is precisely the situation `_check_record` in `item_resume.py:224` guards against (`--decision accept` requires `flagKind == review_unresolved`), so such an item cannot be accepted, only retried — and a retry would reimplement it, which the reason explicitly says it must not. The flag kind and the retry semantics disagree.

findings.title: `--decision accept` requires `flagKind == review_unresolved`, but the retry path re-checks the same restriction only for `accept`
findings.description: `_check_record` allows `retry` on any `FLAGGED` or `NOT_RUN` record, including `not_ready` and `dependency`. But `_select_item` re-evaluates the source and, for a `not_ready` slice, the source will return the item *with* `flag_reason` set again — so `item` is found, `_pre_flag` in the executor pre-flags it, and the item is immediately flagged again without running the body. The CLI then reports `FLAGGED` (exit 1) with no explanation of why nothing ran. The refusal is deterministic and knowable at validation time (the stored record already carries `flag_kind`), but the code lets the user spend a run on it.

findings.title: `_flag_kind` classifies every non-exhausted, non-paused failure as `STEP_FAILED`, losing the failing step's nature
findings.description: `_flag_kind` inspects only `final.status`, `final.exhausted`, and the first failed action. A failure whose action is not `branch` is always `STEP_FAILED`, and `failed_step` is set separately in `_execute_each_step` to `item_results[-1].step_name`. But `item_results[-1]` is the *last* inner step, not the *failing* one — `_run_each_item` breaks on the first FAILED/PAUSED inner step, so `item_results[-1]` is indeed the failing step. However, when the failure is a `PAUSED` status, `_flag_kind` returns `PAUSED` while `_item_outcome` reports `"paused at step {name}"`; the `failed_step` is still populated. `FlagKind.PAUSED` and `FlagKind.STEP_FAILED` are then indistinguishable from `review_unresolved` for a consumer that wants to know whether a human checkpoint is waiting — the `failed_step` field carries it, but the kind does not distinguish "paused waiting for a human at a checkpoint" from "paused by a review gate".

findings.title: `_locked` closes the coroutine only when the lock fails, leaking a coroutine on other exit paths
The run lock is taken on `os.getcwd()`, not on the pipeline's actual working directory
findings.description: `_take_run_lock` calls `project_run_lock(os.getcwd())`. `_git_dir(cwd)` then runs `git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-dir` in that directory. If the user invokes `sq run` from a subdirectory of the repo, `git rev-parse --git-dir` resolves to the repo's `.git` directory — correct. But if the user invokes it from *outside* any repository, `_git_dir` raises `GitEnvironmentError`, which `_take_run_lock` converts to `typer.Exit(2)` — a mutating pipeline can no longer be run outside a git checkout at all. Since the lock's whole purpose is to serialize runs within one checkout, refusing to run when there is no checkout is arguably right, but this is a behaviour change with no test covering "not a git repo" for the CLI path (only `run_lock.py` unit-level), and it changes the exit code from the pipeline's own error handling to a lock error.

findings.title: `pipeline_mutates` does not recognize `commit` as a mutating step type
findings.description: `_MUTATING_STEP_TYPES` contains `DESIGN`, `TASKS`, `IMPLEMENT`, `DEVLOG`, `BRANCH` — but not `COMMIT`. There is no `StepTypeName.COMMIT` (the registry lists `DISPATCH`, `COMPACT`, `SUMMARY`, `REVIEW`, `GATE` etc.), and commit is an *action* rather than a step type, so this is defensible. However, `design`/`tasks`/`implement`/`devlog` are listed as mutating while `summary` and `compact` (which write documents to disk and, per `emit: [rotate]`, rotate session state) are not. More importantly, the `_MUTATING_STEP_TYPES` list is a hand-maintained duplicate of the step-type taxonomy; a new mutating step type added later will silently run without the lock. The project guideline "Never scatter comparison values across code… Changing a value should require editing exactly one place" applies.

findings.title: `run_lock._step_mutates` reads nested steps with a shape assumption that does not match `unpack_inner_steps`
findings.description: `_step_mutates` assumes nested steps are `list[dict[str, {step_type: config}]]` and iterates `for inner_type, inner_config in raw.items()`. But `unpack_inner_steps` (used by the executor) is the canonical parser for that shape, and the `each`/`loop` step bodies in `implement-plan.yaml` are indeed single-key dicts, so the shape matches today. The problem is that `_step_mutates` re-implements the shape knowledge instead of reusing `unpack_inner_steps`, and it silently ignores any nested shape it does not recognise (`inner_config` not a dict → `inner = {}`). A nested `each` body that contains a `branch` step inside a non-dict config would be missed and the run would proceed without the lock. Reusing `unpack_inner_steps` would keep one parser.

findings.title: `resume_item`'s `_Stop` handler logs at WARNING for `REJECTED` but the `OSError` path logs nothing
findings.description: The `except OSError` branch returns a `ResumeOutcome` without any log record at all. The project's Failure-Mode Enumeration rule requires each identified failure mode to be *observable* (log at WARNING+). The report-write failure is observable via `batch_report._write_atomic`'s `_logger.exception`, but only when the failure comes from that function — a different `OSError` source would be entirely silent apart from the returned message.

findings.title: `item_resume.py` is 335 lines and mixes validation, git preconditions, source re-selection, and outcome formatting
findings.description: The module has one clear reason to change (implementing item resume) but exceeds the project's "~300 lines, functions to ~50 lines" guidance and bundles four distinct responsibilities: request validation (`_validate`, `_single_each_step`, `_check_record`), git preconditioning (`_git_precondition`), source re-selection and reconciliation (`_select_item`, `_reconcile`, `_open_dependencies`), and param rebuilding (`item_params`). `_resume_locked` orchestrates them but the reconciliation path (`_reconcile` mutating `run.report.records` directly and writing the report) duplicates the report-update responsibility that `ItemRerun.replace` provides for the normal path.

findings.title: `_reconcile` writes the report through `run.report.write(...)` while the normal path writes through the executor's `_write_each_report`, producing two different write paths
findings.description: The reconciled path mutates `run.report.records[position]` and calls `run.report.write(run.report_path.parent)` directly (synchronously, on the event loop — blocking I/O, unlike `_write_each_report` which uses `asyncio.to_thread`). The normal path goes through `ItemRerun.replace` → executor → `_write_each_report` → `asyncio.to_thread`. Two write paths for the same artifact means the blocking-I/O rule in the Python guide ("Any async def function that calls synchronous code must guarantee that the synchronous code runs in <1ms") is violated on the reconcile path, and the two paths can diverge in logging behaviour.

findings.title: `item_params` drops stored reserved keys with `params.pop(key, None) is not None`, so a stored key with a falsy value is silently kept
findings.description:
```python
dropped = sorted(key for key in RESERVED_PARAMS if params.pop(key, None) is not None)
```
`params.pop(key, None)` removes the key in all cases — the `is not None` only decides whether it is *reported* as dropped. So `{"override_instructions": ""}` is removed but not reported. That is actually the desired outcome for the params dict, but the log line then under-reports: a stored empty `override_instructions` is dropped silently with no WARNING, contradicting the docstring ("Reserved keys stored in run state … are dropped with a WARNING"). The reporting predicate and the removal predicate disagree.

findings.title: `check_item_flags` rejects `--decision`/`--instructions` without `--item`, but `run()` still accepts `--resume` with `--instructions` in other paths
findings.description: `check_item_flags` reports "--decision and --instructions require --item" when either is given without `--item`. This couples two unrelated options into one message and does not name which one was wrong. The project's rules require that a message identify the actual refusal. A user passing only `--instructions` is told about `--decision` too.

findings.title: New test helper files under `tests/` are not named `test_*.py` and are collected as shared fixtures without a `conftest.py`
findings.description: `tests/pipeline/item_resume_support.py` is a non-test module imported explicitly by test files (`from tests.pipeline.item_resume_support import ...`). It imports `from tests.conftest import run_test_git`, i.e. a test module imports from `conftest.py` directly — the standard pytest convention is for shared helpers to live *in* `conftest.py` (or a non-`test_` helper module that does not import from `conftest`). The Python guide says "Use `conftest.py` for shared fixtures; keep individual test files clean." The helper also defines a `Project` dataclass and a `body_runner` factory that returns an untyped function (`# type: ignore[no-untyped-def]`), weakening the strict-mode guarantee for the item-resume test suite — the very tests that cover the most safety-critical new code.

findings.title: The load-test tier required by the Python rules is absent for the new concurrency-adjacent paths
findings.description: The Python rules require "any code on the simulation, network, concurrency, or environment-layer paths requires at least one load test exercising a realistic configuration." This slice adds a process-level concurrency primitive (`project_run_lock` with `flock`) whose whole purpose is serialising concurrent runs, and the executor now writes the report after *every* item (`_write_each_report(report, runs_dir, final=False)`), doubling the write volume for a large batch. The new tests exercise the lock only single-threaded (one holder, one contender) and never assert a latency or resource bound for the per-item report rewrite. There is no `tests/load/` coverage for either.

findings.title: `_write_each_report` now runs after every item, and each write re-serialises the whole report
findings.description: `report.write` renders the full Markdown (including `yaml.safe_dump` of the frontmatter) *and* the full JSON, then atomically writes both files. Doing this after every item is O(n²) in the number of items for the lifetime of a batch: item *k* writes *k* records. For a plan with hundreds of slices this is hundreds of full re-serialisations. The requirement (a report exists after every item) can be met without re-rendering everything each time, or at least the cost should be measured against a realistic plan size.

findings.title: The `resume_item` CLI path bypasses the `StateManager` runs-dir configuration used by the pipeline that wrote the report
findings.description: `handle_item_resume` constructs `StateManager()` with no `runs_dir`, so it reads from the default `~/.config/squadron/runs`. `_validate` then derives the report path as `state_manager.runs_dir / f"{run_id}.{each.name}.report.json"`. The report, however, was written by the original run into `StateManager(runs_dir=runs_dir).runs_dir` (executor.py `_write_each_report`), which is the same default *unless* the original run used a custom `runs_dir`. The run state file is found in the default dir, but a report written elsewhere would not be — the two must agree, and nothing enforces or documents that. A run created with a custom `runs_dir` is silently unresumable via the CLI.

findings.title: `handle_item_resume` catches `typer.Exit` and rewrites it to `HALTED`, masking the specific exit code
findings.description:
```python
except typer.Exit as exc:
    rprint(f"[red]Item {escape(item)} did not finish (exit {exc.exit_code}).[/red]")
    raise typer.Exit(int(ResumeExit.HALTED)) from None
```
`_run_pipeline_sdk` raises `typer.Exit(1)` for a classification failure (a configuration error, `REJECTED`-shaped) and `typer.Exit(1)` for a lost session. Both are flattened to `HALTED` (3), and `from None` discards the original chain. The `ResumeExit` table is a documented contract for automated callers ("for an automated caller (D8)"); collapsing distinct causes into one code makes that contract unusable for routing.

findings.title: Reserved control-param keys are single-sourced and rejected at every entry point
findings.description: `OVERRIDE_INSTRUCTIONS` and `ACCEPT_DECISION` are defined once in `control_params.py` and referenced from `dispatch.py`, `executor.py`, `loader.py` (`validate_pipeline`), `run.py` (`_apply_param_overrides`) and `item_resume.py`. The rejection message is produced by one function (`reserved_param_error`), so the CLI error, the pipeline-validation error, and the item-resume refusal cannot drift apart. Tests in `tests/pipeline/test_control_params.py` cover both the CLI and the pipeline-declaration paths.

findings.title: The batch report's JSON sidecar is written atomically and validated on read
findings.description: `_write_atomic` writes to a sibling temp file and renames it over the target, so a reader never sees a partial file and a failed write leaves the previous report intact. `BatchReport.load` catches `FileNotFoundError`, `OSError`, `UnicodeDecodeError` and `json.JSONDecodeError`, and rejects a mismatched `schemaVersion` with a message naming both versions. `tests/pipeline/test_batch_report.py` exercises the round trip, the version mismatch, the unparseable file, the missing file, and the failed-write-keeps-the-old-report case (including that the error is logged at ERROR).

findings.title: `StateManager.list_runs` no longer mistakes a batch report for a run state
findings.description: The `REPORT_JSON_SUFFIX` filter is applied before `_load_raw`, so the sidecar is skipped silently instead of producing a "Skipping unreadable state file" warning. The suffix constant lives in `batch_report.py` and is imported rather than duplicated, so the writer and the reader cannot disagree on the filename. `tests/pipeline/test_state.py` asserts both the run list and the absence of the warning.

findings.title: The `each` step records unreached items as `not_run` when a git fault halts the batch
findings.description: `_finish_each_report` distinguishes the in-flight item (recorded as flagged with the fault's own message) from the items the halt never reached (recorded as `NOT_RUN` via `BatchItemRecord.not_run`). `FlagKind` and `ItemOutcome` are closed enums, `BatchReport.to_json` counts every outcome, and `tests/pipeline/test_each_report_writes.py` asserts the exact four-row outcome/flagKind/reason sequence and the counts, plus that a report already existed after item 1 (before item 2 ran).

findings.title: The item-resume flow is covered by a substantial, behaviour-focused test suite
findings.description: The new tests cover the retry path (instructions injected into the dispatch prompt, branch work kept, merge performed), the accept path (no rounds run, one review, merged), a retry that flags again, a `not_run` item resuming, an unknown git state halting mid-item, a failed report rewrite halting with the old report intact, and the reconciliation case. The fakes exercise real git moves in a temporary repository, so the assertions are about observable behaviour rather than implementation details. `tests/pipeline/test_item_resume_validation.py` additionally asserts that a refused request touches nothing (branch, refs, and report bytes are snapshotted before and after).
